question: A team keeps its infrastructure definitions in Git. Which IaC benefit does this most directly provide?
options: Automatic patching of operating systems on every managed server
Guaranteed lower cloud bills because idle resources are removed
No need for a cloud account, because the Git repository itself hosts all of the infrastructure
A full history of infrastructure changes that can be reviewed and rolled back
explanation: Storing IaC in version control gives an auditable history, code review and the ability to roll back to a known-good definition.

question: Which statement correctly contrasts declarative and imperative approaches?
options: Imperative tools always use HCL, while declarative ones use JSON
Declarative defines the steps to run in order; imperative defines only the final end state
Declarative defines the end state; imperative defines the steps to get there
Declarative tools cannot manage dependencies between resources
explanation: Terraform is declarative: you describe what you want and Terraform calculates the actions needed to reach it.

question: Which TWO problems does Infrastructure as Code help reduce? (Choose two)
options: Network latency between cloud regions
Inconsistent environments built by hand
The cost of storage for state files
The need to understand the target platform
Undocumented manual changes to infrastructure
explanation: Codifying infrastructure makes builds consistent and documents every change, reducing snowflake environments and undocumented tweaks.

question: Which approach best helps you detect configuration drift with Terraform?
options: Run terraform plan regularly and review any unexpected changes
Delete the lock file so that every provider is forced to re-read the real infrastructure
Run terraform validate against the production account
Run terraform fmt to compare files with real infrastructure
explanation: terraform plan refreshes state against real infrastructure, so unexpected proposed changes reveal drift. HCP Terraform health assessments can automate this.

question: A configuration was applied successfully. Without any changes, you run terraform plan. What should the plan report?
options: That every resource will be refreshed and replaced
That there are no changes and infrastructure matches the configuration
That all resources will be updated in place to re-sync
That the state file must be migrated before planning
explanation: Terraform is idempotent: if real infrastructure already matches the configuration, the plan reports no changes.

question: Your company uses AWS, Azure and a SaaS monitoring tool. Why is Terraform a good fit?
options: It converts Azure and SaaS resources into AWS resources automatically during each apply
It replaces each platform's API with its own hosted service
It can manage all three with one workflow through their providers
It only needs credentials for one of the three platforms
explanation: Providers let Terraform manage many platforms using the same language and plan/apply workflow.

question: Which of the following is stored in Terraform state?
options: Mappings between resource addresses and real object IDs, plus their attributes
A copy of every provider plugin used by the configuration
Only the names of the resources, with no attribute values
The full history of every plan that has ever been run
explanation: State binds configuration addresses to remote object IDs and records attributes and metadata such as dependencies.

question: Resource B references an attribute of resource A. What does Terraform do?
options: Creates both in parallel and retries B if it fails
Creates A before B because of the implicit dependency
Creates B before A because B appears first in the file
Requires depends_on before it will create either resource
explanation: References create implicit dependencies in the graph, so Terraform creates A first. depends_on is only needed for hidden dependencies.

question: Which task is Terraform best suited to compared with a configuration management tool?
options: Restarting an application service when its config changes
Installing patches on hundreds of existing virtual machines
Creating a VPC, subnets and a load balancer from scratch
Editing a config file on a running server every few minutes
explanation: Terraform focuses on provisioning and lifecycle of infrastructure; configuration management tools focus on software and settings inside servers.

question: What file extension marks a Terraform configuration file written in JSON syntax?
options: .json.tf
.tfjson
.tfvars.yaml
.tf.json
explanation: Terraform reads .tf files (HCL) and .tf.json files (JSON syntax). .tfvars.json is used for variable values.

question: A required_providers entry has source = "hashicorp/aws". What does this address refer to?
options: A local folder named hashicorp/aws next to the configuration
The AWS console endpoint that Terraform logs in to
The aws provider in the hashicorp namespace on the public Terraform Registry
A GitHub repository called aws that is owned by the hashicorp organization on github.com
explanation: A source address is [hostname/]namespace/type; the hostname defaults to registry.terraform.io.

question: Which block correctly pins the AWS provider to version 5.x?
options: terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.0" } } }
variable "aws" { version = "~> 5.0" }
terraform { required_version = "aws ~> 5.0" }
provider "aws" { source = "hashicorp/aws", required_version = "~> 5.0", region = var.region }
explanation: Provider sources and version constraints belong in required_providers inside the terraform block. required_version constrains the Terraform CLI itself.

question: Should the .terraform.lock.hcl file be committed to version control?
options: Yes, so everyone gets the same provider versions
No, it contains secrets and must be ignored
Only when you use the local backend for state
No, because it is regenerated from scratch every time anyone runs terraform plan
explanation: HashiCorp recommends committing the dependency lock file so all users and CI install the same provider versions and checksums.

question: A resource must be created with a provider configuration that has alias = "west". Which argument goes on the resource?
options: region = aws.west
provider = aws.west
alias = "west" (set on the resource)
provider = "west"
explanation: Resources select a non-default provider configuration with provider = <PROVIDER>.<ALIAS>.

question: Which version constraint allows 1.2.0 up to, but not including, 1.3.0?
explanation: ~> allows only the rightmost given component to increase: ~> 1.2.0 means >= 1.2.0 and < 1.3.0, whereas ~> 1.2 allows up to < 2.0.

question: Your lock file pins an old provider version that still satisfies your constraints. How do you move to the newest allowed version?
options: Run terraform init -upgrade
Run terraform providers lock -reset
Run terraform get -update=false
Run terraform apply -refresh-only
explanation: terraform init -upgrade ignores the locked versions, picks the newest versions allowed by the constraints, and updates the lock file.

question: Which TWO statements about provider configuration are correct? (Choose two)
options: A configuration can contain multiple configurations of the same provider using alias
Every provider must be published by HashiCorp to be installed
Terraform can only use one provider per configuration
Provider plugins are downloaded during terraform init
Providers must be configured inside each resource block
explanation: Aliases allow multiple configurations of one provider, and init downloads the provider plugins the configuration needs.

question: Which is the safest way to give Terraform AWS credentials in a CI pipeline?
options: Use short-lived credentials from the CI platform, e.g. OIDC or env vars
Put the access key in a default value of a variable block
Commit an access key in terraform.tfvars so every pipeline run can read it from the repository
Store the access key in an output so later jobs can reuse it
explanation: Avoid hardcoding secrets. Short-lived credentials or environment variables keep secrets out of code, state outputs and version control.

question: You use an import block to bring an existing S3 bucket under management. What else must exist?
options: A data block that reads the same bucket by name
A matching resource block for the bucket in your configuration
A moved block pointing from the old address to the new one
Nothing else; the import block creates the resource block
explanation: An import block needs a resource block at its 'to' address. You can write it yourself or generate it with terraform plan -generate-config-out.

question: You no longer want Terraform to manage a database, but it must keep running. Which command removes it from state only?
options: terraform destroy -target=aws_db_instance.main
terraform state rm aws_db_instance.main
terraform taint aws_db_instance.main
terraform apply -replace=aws_db_instance.main
explanation: terraform state rm forgets the object without destroying it. A removed block with destroy = false does the same declaratively.

question: Which command shows the attributes of a single resource in state?
options: terraform state show aws_instance.web
terraform console --show aws_instance.web
terraform state list aws_instance.web -full
terraform output aws_instance.web
explanation: terraform state show <address> prints the recorded attributes of one resource instance; state list only lists addresses.

question: Which TF_LOG level produces the most detailed output?
options: TRACE
DEBUG
VERBOSE
INFO
explanation: TF_LOG accepts TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN and ERROR (or JSON). TRACE is the most verbose.

question: terraform taint is deprecated. What is the recommended replacement?
options: terraform state rm followed by terraform import
terraform apply -replace=ADDRESS
terraform refresh -replace=ADDRESS
terraform plan -destroy -target=ADDRESS
explanation: Use -replace on plan or apply to force replacement; you see the effect in the plan before it happens.

question: Inside terraform console you type var.region. What happens?
options: It prints the current value of the region variable
It changes the region of every provider configuration
It opens the variables.tf file for editing
It returns an error because console cannot read variables
explanation: terraform console evaluates expressions, including variables, locals and resource attributes from state.

question: You move a resource into a module, from aws_s3_bucket.logs to module.storage.aws_s3_bucket.logs. How do you avoid recreating it?
options: Set lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } on it
Run terraform init -migrate-state
Add an import block pointing at the new address
Add a moved block with from and to addresses
explanation: moved blocks tell Terraform the object has a new address, so it updates state instead of destroying and recreating.

question: A removed block includes lifecycle { destroy = false }. What happens on apply?
options: Terraform errors because removed cannot use lifecycle
The resource leaves state but the real object is kept
The resource stays in state but is no longer refreshed
The resource is destroyed and removed from state
explanation: With destroy = false, the removed block forgets the resource without destroying the real infrastructure.

question: You run terraform plan in a directory that calls three modules. Which one is the root module?
options: Whichever of the three called modules is listed first in the configuration files
A special module downloaded during terraform init
The module with the most resources in it
The configuration in the directory where you ran the command
explanation: Every configuration has a root module: the .tf files in the working directory. The modules it calls are child modules.

question: A module called "db" uses count = 2 and declares an output named endpoint. How do you reference the first instance's endpoint?
options: module.db.endpoint[0]
module.db[0].endpoint
output.db[0].endpoint
db[0].endpoint
explanation: With count on a module block, each instance is addressed by index: module.<NAME>[INDEX].<OUTPUT>.

question: Which module source supports the version argument in the module block?
options: A local path, e.g. "./modules/vpc"
An HTTP URL to a zip archive of the module
A Git URL, e.g. "git::https://example.com/vpc.git"
A module from the Terraform Registry, e.g. "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
explanation: version only works for registry modules (public or private). For Git sources, pin with ?ref= in the URL.

question: A child module declares variable "instance_type" with no default. What happens if the parent doesn't set it?
options: Terraform uses null and creates the resource anyway
Terraform reads the value from the parent's variables of the same name
Terraform reports an error that a required argument is missing
Terraform prompts for the value interactively inside the module
explanation: A module variable without a default is required; the module block must set it or Terraform errors.

question: You change the version of a registry module in a module block. What must you run before plan?
options: terraform state pull
terraform fmt -recursive
terraform get -refresh
terraform init (or init -upgrade)
explanation: Module sources and versions are installed by terraform init. Use -upgrade to pick a newer version within the constraint.

question: Which TWO are good practices when writing reusable modules? (Choose two)
options: Store each module's state inside the module folder
Avoid version constraints on registry modules
Hardcode provider credentials inside the module
Return useful values through outputs
Expose configurable values as input variables
explanation: Inputs make modules configurable and outputs expose results to callers; credentials and state don't belong in modules.

question: How do you pin a Git-sourced module to tag v2.0.0?
options: source = "git::https://example.com/net.git@v2.0.0"
source = "git::https://example.com/net.git?ref=v2.0.0"
source = "git::https://example.com/net.git#tag=v2.0.0"
source = "git::https://example.com/net.git" with version = "v2.0.0"
explanation: Git sources select a branch, tag or commit with the ref query parameter. The version argument only applies to registry modules.

question: A child module creates a subnet. The parent wants its ID. What must the child contain?
options: variable "subnet_id" { default = aws_subnet.this.id }
locals { export = aws_subnet.this.id }
data "aws_subnet" "this" { export = true }
output "subnet_id" { value = aws_subnet.this.id }
explanation: Only declared outputs are visible to the calling module, as module.<name>.<output>.

question: Which command belongs to the 'Plan' stage of the core workflow?
options: terraform fmt
terraform init
terraform output
terraform plan
explanation: Write → Plan → Apply. terraform plan previews the changes before you apply them.

question: terraform validate passes. Which of these could still go wrong at apply time?
options: A resource block missing a required argument
The cloud API rejects a value, e.g. an invalid instance type
An unclosed brace in main.tf
A reference to a variable that isn't declared
explanation: validate checks syntax and internal consistency offline. It doesn't call provider APIs, so invalid real-world values only fail during plan or apply.

question: In CI you want to fail the build if files aren't formatted, without changing them. Which command?
options: terraform plan -check
terraform fmt -check
terraform validate -fmt
terraform fmt -write=true
explanation: terraform fmt -check exits non-zero when files need formatting, without rewriting them.

question: You run terraform apply tfplan, where tfplan was saved earlier with -out. What happens?
options: Terraform only shows the plan and never applies it
Terraform merges the saved plan with a new one
Terraform discards the saved plan, creates a new plan and asks you to approve it again
Terraform applies that exact saved plan without asking for approval
explanation: Applying a saved plan file performs exactly those actions, and doesn't prompt for approval because you already reviewed it.

question: How can you preview what terraform destroy would remove before running it?
options: terraform show -remove
terraform validate -destroy
terraform plan -destroy
terraform state list -destroy
explanation: terraform plan -destroy produces a speculative destroy plan for review.

question: Which TWO statements about terraform init are true? (Choose two)
options: It must be run after every apply
It creates resources defined in the root module
It deletes the existing state file
It installs required providers and modules
It is safe to run multiple times
explanation: init is idempotent and prepares the working directory: backend, providers and modules. It never creates infrastructure.

question: Someone resized a VM manually. You want state to record the new size without changing the VM. Which command?
options: terraform apply -refresh-only
terraform plan -target
terraform apply -replace=ADDRESS
terraform state push
explanation: A refresh-only apply updates state to match real infrastructure without proposing changes to resources.

question: In a plan, what does a resource marked with ~ mean?
options: It will be read as a data source
It will be created
It will be destroyed and recreated
It will be updated in place
explanation: ~ means update in place, + means create, - means destroy, and -/+ means replace.

question: A tag was deleted manually from a resource Terraform manages. What will terraform apply do?
options: Fail until you run terraform refresh
Ignore it because tags are not tracked
Remove the tag from the configuration file
Add the tag back to match the configuration
explanation: Terraform reconciles real infrastructure to the configuration, so it restores the tag unless ignore_changes covers it.

question: Which file holds the previous state after a local apply?
options: .terraform/state.prev
terraform.tfstate.backup
terraform.lock.backup
terraform.tfstate.old
explanation: With the local backend, Terraform keeps the prior state in terraform.tfstate.backup.

question: A previous apply crashed and the state is still locked. Which command releases it?
options: terraform apply -lock=false -force
terraform state rm -lock
terraform init -unlock
terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID
explanation: force-unlock removes a stuck lock using its ID. Use it only when you're sure no other run is in progress.

question: Why should state files never be committed to a public Git repository?
options: Terraform deletes state found inside a Git repository
Git cannot store JSON files larger than 1 MB
They are encrypted and unreadable without the original key
They can contain secrets such as passwords in plain text
explanation: State can hold sensitive values in plain text. Use a secure remote backend with access controls and encryption.

question: A networking configuration exposes output "vpc_id". How does another configuration read it through terraform_remote_state named net?
options: data.terraform_remote_state.net.outputs.vpc_id
data.terraform_remote_state.net.outputs["vpc_id"].value
module.net.outputs.vpc_id
data.terraform_remote_state.net.vpc_id
explanation: Root module outputs are available under the outputs attribute of the terraform_remote_state data source.

question: You switch from the local backend to S3 and want existing state copied across. Which command?
options: terraform init -migrate-state
terraform init -reconfigure
terraform state push s3
terraform apply -backend-config=s3.tfbackend
explanation: -migrate-state copies existing state to the new backend; -reconfigure would ignore the old state.

question: Which command creates and switches to a new CLI workspace named dev?
options: terraform workspace new dev
terraform init -workspace=dev
terraform env add dev
terraform workspace select -create
explanation: terraform workspace new creates a workspace and switches to it; workspace select switches to an existing one.

question: Why is editing terraform.tfstate by hand discouraged?
options: It is easy to corrupt it or break the mapping to real resources
Terraform refuses to read any state that has line breaks
Hand edits are always reverted on the next terraform init
State files are stored in a binary format, so ordinary text editors cannot open them
explanation: State is JSON, but manual edits risk corruption. Use terraform state commands or moved/import/removed blocks.

question: Which backend type is NOT a valid way to store state remotely?
options: s3
gcs
azurerm
github
explanation: s3, azurerm and gcs are remote backends. There is no github backend; HCP Terraform uses the cloud block.

question: When are CLI workspaces a poor fit?
options: When you want separate state for each feature branch
When the same code is deployed with small variable changes
When testing a short-lived copy of the same configuration
When environments need different credentials and strong isolation
explanation: CLI workspaces share one backend and configuration, so they don't isolate credentials or access. Separate configurations or backends are better for that.

question: A variable is set in terraform.tfvars and in a *.auto.tfvars file. Which value wins?
options: Terraform reports a conflict error
The default in the variable block
The *.auto.tfvars value
The terraform.tfvars value
explanation: Precedence (lowest to highest): env vars, terraform.tfvars, *.auto.tfvars (lexical order), then -var and -var-file on the command line.

question: You need for_each over a list of strings. What is the usual way to make it valid?
options: Wrap it with length()
Wrap it with flatten()
Wrap it with tomap()
Wrap it with toset()
explanation: for_each accepts a map or a set of strings; toset() converts a list (and removes duplicates).

question: Which lifecycle argument makes Terraform skip updates when a specific attribute changes outside Terraform?
options: prevent_destroy
replace_triggered_by
create_before_destroy
ignore_changes
explanation: ignore_changes tells Terraform to ignore differences in the listed attributes when planning updates.

question: Which lifecycle argument forces a resource to be replaced when another resource changes?
options: depends_on
create_before_destroy
replace_triggered_by
ignore_changes
explanation: replace_triggered_by replaces the resource when any referenced resource or attribute changes.

question: An output references a sensitive variable. What must you do?
options: Nothing, because output values are never displayed in the terminal after an apply
Move the output into a separate module
Encrypt the value with the base64encode function
Mark the output sensitive = true, or Terraform errors
explanation: Terraform requires outputs that contain sensitive values to be marked sensitive, so they're redacted in CLI output.

question: A bucket policy must exist before an application uses it, but nothing references the policy. What should you add?
options: depends_on on the application resource
An import block for the bucket
A moved block for the policy
lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }
explanation: depends_on declares hidden dependencies that Terraform can't infer from references.

question: Inside dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.rules ... }, how do you refer to the current element?
options: each.value
ingress.value
dynamic.value
var.rules.value
explanation: In a dynamic block the iterator is named after the block label by default, so use ingress.value and ingress.key.

question: What is the main difference between a resource block and a data block?
options: Data sources must always be inside a module
Resources cannot reference values from data sources
Resources are created and managed; data sources only read
Resources only read existing objects; data sources create and manage new infrastructure
explanation: data blocks query existing information without managing its lifecycle. Resource blocks create, update and destroy objects.

question: You repeat the same tags expression in ten resources. What is the best way to define it once?
options: An output value
A provisioner
A local value
A data source
explanation: locals name an expression once so you can reuse it throughout the module.

question: What does { for k, v in var.users : k => upper(v) } produce?
options: A list of uppercased keys
A set of the original values
A single uppercased string
A map with the same keys and uppercased values
explanation: A for expression in braces builds a map; k => upper(v) keeps each key and transforms the value.

question: What does length(["a", "b", "c"]) return?
options: "abc"
An error
explanation: length returns the number of elements in a list, map or set, or characters in a string.

question: How do you reference the id of a data source data "aws_vpc" "main"?
options: var.aws_vpc.main.id
data.main.aws_vpc.id
data.aws_vpc.main.id
aws_vpc.main.id
explanation: Data sources are referenced with the data. prefix: data.<TYPE>.<NAME>.<ATTRIBUTE>.

question: When does Terraform evaluate a postcondition on a resource?
options: Only during terraform destroy operations
Only when terraform fmt rewrites the configuration
Before terraform init downloads any providers
After the resource is planned or applied, to check the result
explanation: Preconditions check assumptions before an object is evaluated; postconditions check guarantees about the result after it.

question: A variable validation block's condition evaluates to false. What happens?
options: Terraform stops with the error_message you defined
Terraform logs a warning and continues
Terraform uses the default value instead
Terraform deletes the variable from state
explanation: A failed validation condition produces an error using error_message and stops the operation.

question: Which kind of value is designed never to be stored in plan or state files?
options: Output values
Ephemeral values
Local values
Sensitive values
explanation: Ephemeral variables, outputs and resources (Terraform 1.10+) are not persisted to plan or state. Sensitive values are still stored.

question: A resource uses for_each over a map. How do you reference the current map key?
options: each.index
each.key
count.index
self.key
explanation: With for_each, each.key and each.value refer to the current element; count.index is only for count.

question: Why is for_each often preferred over count for a set of similar resources?
options: count cannot be used with variables or locals
for_each instances don't need to be stored in state
for_each creates resources faster than count because instances are applied in parallel
Removing one item doesn't shift the addresses of the others
explanation: count addresses by index, so removing a middle item shifts later ones and causes churn. for_each addresses by stable keys.

question: Which TWO files does Terraform load automatically for variable values? (Choose two)
options: prod.auto.tfvars
outputs.tf
variables.tf.bak
values.tfvars
terraform.tfvars
explanation: terraform.tfvars(.json) and *.auto.tfvars(.json) load automatically. Other .tfvars files need -var-file.

question: Which type constraint describes a list where every element is an object with a name string and port number?
options: tuple(string, number)
list(map(string, number))
object(list({ name = string, port = number }))
list(object({ name = string, port = number }))
explanation: Combine collection and structural types: list(object({...})). map() takes one element type.

question: In HCP Terraform, what is a project?
options: A way to group related workspaces and manage access to them
A single configuration file stored in HCP Terraform
A personal sandbox that cannot contain workspaces
A replacement for the terraform block in configuration
explanation: Projects organize workspaces and let you grant team access at the project level.

question: A Sentinel policy with enforcement level hard-mandatory fails. What happens to the run?
options: The policy is ignored for that run
The run continues with a warning
The run stops and cannot be overridden
An organization owner can override the failure and let the run continue
explanation: Hard-mandatory failures block the run. Soft-mandatory can be overridden by authorized users; advisory only warns.

question: How do you reference a module from your organization's private registry in HCP Terraform?
options: source = "registry.terraform.io/private/ORG/NAME"
source = "private::ORG/NAME"
source = "tfe://ORG/NAME"
source = "app.terraform.io/ORG/NAME/PROVIDER"
explanation: Private registry modules use the hostname-prefixed address app.terraform.io/<ORG>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER>.

question: Where are values from a variable set applied?
options: Only to modules in the private registry
To every workspace or project the set is assigned to
Only to CLI-driven runs on your local machine
Only to the single workspace that originally created the variable set
explanation: Variable sets can be applied globally or to selected projects and workspaces, avoiding duplicate variables.

question: In a VCS-driven workspace, what does opening a pull request usually trigger?
options: A destroy of all resources in the workspace
An immediate apply to production with no review
A speculative plan whose result is shown on the pull request
Nothing until someone runs terraform plan locally
explanation: Pull requests trigger speculative (plan-only) runs; merging to the tracked branch triggers a full run.

question: Your infrastructure is in a private data centre that HCP Terraform cannot reach. What feature helps?
options: Run triggers
HCP Terraform agents
Variable sets
The public module registry
explanation: Agents run inside your network and poll HCP Terraform for work, so plans and applies can reach private infrastructure.

question: When is cost estimation shown in an HCP Terraform run?
options: Before terraform init runs
Only after the apply finishes
Only in the monthly billing email
After the plan, before the apply
explanation: Cost estimation runs after the plan so you can review the cost impact before applying.

question: What does drift detection in HCP Terraform health assessments do?
options: Upgrades provider versions when a new one is released
Automatically reverts any manual changes it finds
Blocks anyone from making changes in the cloud console
Checks regularly whether real infrastructure has changed from state
explanation: Health assessments run periodic refresh-only plans and notify you of drift; they don't fix it automatically.

question: Which TWO ways can you start a run in HCP Terraform? (Choose two)
options: Pushing a commit to a connected VCS branch
Editing the lock file in the workspace UI
Uploading state with terraform state push
Sending an SMS to HCP Terraform
Running terraform plan from the CLI with a cloud block
explanation: Runs can be CLI-driven, VCS-driven or API-driven. Pushing state doesn't start a run.
